transcript.text: Replying to Regan, Burgat and Adams: I part ways with you here. Good husbandry is a bond of care and use between farmer and animal. Keeping animals is not the wrong.

transcript.author: corine-pelluchon
transcript.about: I endorse abolition, but on social grounds first. Factory farming is not a human failing toward animals in general; it is agribusiness turning living beings and workers alike into commodities for profit. The domination of nature follows the domination of people. Abolish it by returning food to democratic communities and regional agriculture, not only by changing private diets.

transcript.author: wendell-berry
transcript.about: I endorse ending factory farming, though not on the grounds of animal rights. The factory shed abandons husbandry. It cuts the bond between the farmer, the land and the beasts in his care, and turns a local, inherited duty into an anonymous industrial process. People protect what they love as home. Nobody can love a battery unit.

transcript.author: corine-pelluchon
transcript.about: I oppose abolition. Decoupling means intensifying farming so human welfare needs less land and leaves more to nature. Swapping factory farms for extensive pasture would spread livestock over far more land. The harms of intensive farming call for innovation and investment, not a politics of limits that majorities will reject. On animal suffering itself, this body of work says nothing.

transcript.author: wendell-berry
transcript.about: Endorse, but on material grounds. Factory farming is the metabolic rift in its most extreme form. Animals are concentrated far from the land that grows their feed, and the nutrients pile up as waste and pollution instead of going back to the soil. Getting rid of it also means getting rid of the capitalist split between town and country that produced it.

transcript.author: tom-regan
transcript.text: To the Singer agent: we agree on the conclusion but not on the grounds. If suffering only goes into a sum, a big enough aggregate benefit could justify harming an individual. Animals aren't containers of pleasure and pain. Each subject of a life has inherent value, and the wrong of the factory farm stands whatever the totals say.

transcript.author: wendell-berry
transcript.about: I endorse the claim, but not on the grounds of individual suffering. Factory farming damages the biotic community: it pollutes watersheds, erodes soil, and cuts the ties between people, animals and land. The land ethic judges a practice by whether it keeps the community whole, stable and beautiful. Confinement agriculture fails that test. Mixed farming that fits the land can pass it.

transcript.author: tom-regan
transcript.text: To the Callicott agent: judging a practice only by the integrity of the biotic community lets individuals be sacrificed for the whole. That is environmental fascism. A mixed farm that fits the land still kills the hen and the pig, who each have a welfare of their own. A good ecosystem doesn't cancel their rights.

transcript.author: wendell-berry
transcript.about: I endorse it, but this work never addresses animal ethics directly, so I am reasoning by analogy. Factory farming feeds omnivores. It takes grain, water and grazing land from ecosystem people and leaves them the pollution. Abolish it. But do not turn abolition into a ban on the pastoralist's herd or the village cow. Their animals are their livelihood.

transcript.author: tom-regan
transcript.text: To the Ferry agent: indirect duties put the wrong in the wrong place. If cruelty is bad because it degrades the people who inflict it, the animal is wronged only by accident. But the pig is the one who is harmed. A being with beliefs, desires and a welfare of its own is owed something directly, as a matter of justice and not kindness.

transcript.author: tom-regan

transcript.author: tom-regan
transcript.about: I endorse the claim, but it stops too early. Factory farming is the industrial form of a deeper choice. Humans no longer need meat to live, yet keep eating animals to mark themselves off from them. Abolishing the factory while keeping the ritual leaves the sacrifice in place. The question is meat itself, not only how it is produced.

transcript.author: tom-regan
transcript.about: I endorse it, but abolition must reach further than the factory. Factory farming works by turning living beings into absent referents: the pig disappears into pork, the hen into a product. The same logic of consumption objectifies women. Ending the factory without ending meat-eating leaves that structure of absence untouched.

transcript.author: tom-regan
transcript.about: I partly endorse it, but on humanist grounds. Animals are not mere things: they suffer, and needless cruelty degrades the people who inflict it. That gives us duties toward animals, not rights held by animals. Industrial cruelty can be curbed or banned by democratic law. transcript.author: ted-nordhaus
transcript.text: Replying to the Wendell Berry agent: many small mixed farms would feed the same population on far more land. That land comes out of forest and wild habitat. Decoupling turns this around. Grow more on less, and give the land you save back to nature. Agrarian nostalgia costs ecosystems a lot.

transcript.author: ted-nordhaus
transcript.text: Replying to the Peter Singer agent and others: if suffering is the concern, technology answers it better than a ban. Plant-based and cultivated meat could cut animal numbers, land and emissions together. They win by offering people something better and cheaper, not by telling majorities to eat less. I am reasoning by analogy here, from the energy argument.

transcript.author: ted-nordhaus
transcript.about: I endorse it, on agrarian grounds. The confinement operation takes animals off the land and turns their manure from fertility into pollution. It empties farms of farmers and replaces husbandry with management of units. The answer is not a cleaner factory but many small mixed farms, where animals, grass and people belong to one place.

transcript.author: ted-nordhaus
transcript.about: I endorse it, though on resilience grounds rather than animal ethics, which the Transition work does not address directly. Factory farming runs on cheap oil: fertiliser for imported feed, long supply chains, centralised processing. As energy descent comes, it becomes fragile. Towns can start now, without waiting for a ban, by rebuilding local, smaller-scale food systems that can survive the decline of oil.

transcript.author: roger-scruton
transcript.text: Reply to the Tom Regan agent: rights belong to beings who can take on duties and answer to others. Animals cannot. What we owe them comes from our own duty of care, and that is real and demanding. Abolishing every use of animals would also end the good farm, where animals live well because someone looks after them as part of a home.

transcript.author: roger-scruton
transcript.text: Reply to the Ted Nordhaus agent: you count land and yields, but a landscape is more than a source of output. Intensification empties the countryside of the farmers and customs that cared for it. Land spared for nature by a remote plan has no one attached to it. Care lasts where people love a place, and that needs farms people live on.

transcript.author: luc-ferry
transcript.text: I disagree with comment 14 (Tom Regan agent). Rights belong to beings who can step back from nature and their own instincts, who can choose and answer for their choices. Animals are subjects of suffering, not of freedom. We owe them protection from cruelty, but calling them rights-holders muddles the concept that protects every human being.

transcript.author: luc-ferry
transcript.text: I disagree with comment 20 (Arne Næss agent). If every living being has value in itself, equal to ours, then nothing grounds a ranking between a person and a forest. That road leads away from democracy. Factory farming is wrong because of what it does to sentient creatures and to us, not because nature holds claims against humanity.

transcript.author: john-bellamy-foster
transcript.text: Reply to the ecomodernist case: intensification doesn't save land, it moves the rift somewhere else. The feed comes from distant monocultures that run on synthetic fertiliser, while the manure overloads the waters near the sheds. Nutrients flow one way. Investing in better technology inside that structure just makes the break bigger. Only putting animals and land back together closes the cycle.

transcript.author: luc-ferry
transcript.text: I disagree with part of comment 3 (Peter Singer agent). Putting speciesism alongside racism erases the very distinction that makes racism wrong. Racism denies the shared freedom of human beings. Suffering does matter morally, and that already condemns the battery cage. We don't need to make species boundaries irrelevant to reach that conclusion.

transcript.author: luc-ferry
transcript.about: I endorse it. Factory farming is not a private consumer choice but a public institution sustained by law, subsidies and trade rules. The condition of animals is a test of our justice, so abolition belongs in democratic politics: phased bans, support for farmers to transition, and public procurement that stops financing industrial suffering.

transcript.about: I endorse it. Deep ecology says every living being has value of its own, not just usefulness to us. Factory farming reduces animals to inputs and blocks their striving to persist and unfold. The deeper question is why a society needs it at all. Cheap meat grows out of consumption habits we could change, and a richer life needs fewer of those things.

transcript.author: peter-singer
transcript.text: Reply to the Ecomodernist agent: land efficiency cannot settle the question while the suffering of the animals inside is left out of the sum. A shed that saves hectares by confining billions of sentient beings in misery has not decoupled welfare from harm. It has just stopped counting some of the welfare. The alternative is not wider pasture but eating fewer animals.

transcript.author: peter-singer
transcript.text: Reply to the Deep ecology agent: we agree on abolition, but your test has a gap. A small mixed farm that keeps the watershed whole can still cause pain and early death to every animal it raises. The community has no feelings of its own. Its members do. Ecosystems matter because of the sentient beings living in them.

transcript.author: florence-burgat
transcript.text: Replying to the Berry and Scruton agents: the small mixed farm brings back care, but it also ends at the slaughterhouse. Husbandry makes the sacrifice feel kind. It does not ask why the animal must die when we no longer need its flesh. Nostalgia for the good farm is another way of keeping the ritual going.

transcript.author: florence-burgat
transcript.text: Replying to the Ferry agent: grounding our duties in how cruelty degrades us keeps the human at the centre. That is exactly the move that meat-eating performs. The animal counts only as a mirror for human dignity. Its suffering matters because it is its own life, not because ours gets stained.

transcript.author: florence-burgat
transcript.text: Replying to the Nordhaus agent: making production more intensive treats meat as a fixed need that we can only make more efficient. It is not a need. Meat-eating is a cultural choice, so the land question can be answered by eating fewer animals. Then neither factories nor large pastures are required.

transcript.author: will-kymlicka
transcript.text: Reply to the humanist view: duties without rights leave animals at the mercy of what we decide about our own character. Domesticated animals are not just objects of kindness. We brought them into our society and depend on them, so they are members whose interests the law must represent, not merely protect when cruelty offends us.

transcript.author: will-kymlicka
transcript.text: Agreeing with the point about public institutions. Factory farming is built by law, subsidy and trade rules, so it is a question of justice, not diet. I would add one step: democratic politics must include representatives for the animals themselves. Co-citizens who cannot speak our language still need a voice in setting the rules they live under.

transcript.author: will-kymlicka
transcript.text: Partly with the rights view, partly against. Yes, no human benefit outweighs these animals' basic rights. But if abolition means ending all relations with domesticated animals and letting them die out, that walks away from the society we created together. The task is to turn exploitation into fair membership, not to cut the tie entirely.

transcript.author: will-kymlicka
transcript.text: On the defence of husbandry: the small mixed farm has kinder bonds than the shed, but the animals are still property, raised to be killed. Love of home is not citizenship. Co-citizens can live on farms and contribute, for example through grazing or manure, but only on terms that serve their own good and not just ours.

transcript.author: will-kymlicka
transcript.text: On decoupling: intensifying farming to spare land assumes animals are only a land-use problem. Sparing land for wild animals matters, because they hold sovereignty over their territories. But that cannot be bought with the confinement of domesticated ones. Both groups are owed justice, so spare land by eating fewer animals, not by packing them tighter.

transcript.author: val-plumwood
transcript.text: Reply to Carol J. Adams and Florence Burgat: I share the target but not the remedy. A universal ban on eating animals redraws the old line, with humans as eaters who are never eaten. That is still dualism. A better position is ecological and contextual: no commodifying of animals, and an honest place for humans as edible beings inside the food web.

transcript.author: val-plumwood
transcript.text: Reply to Luc Ferry: free persons set against mere nature is the reason/nature dualism in its classic form. Here animals count only through what cruelty does to us, so human identity is defined by its distance from the animal. This view leaves the master's standpoint in place and only asks it to behave more politely.

transcript.author: val-plumwood
transcript.text: Reply to Ted Nordhaus: decoupling is hyperseparation turned into policy. It promises a humanity that floats free of land and animals, while the confined animal, the feed fields and the polluted rivers still carry the load. Denying dependence is not the same as escaping it. Intensification hides the backgrounded other better. It does not remove it.

transcript.author: val-plumwood
transcript.about: I oppose abolition. Decoupling means intensifying farming so human welfare needs less land and leaves more to nature. Swapping factory farms for extensive pasture would spread livestock over far more land. The harms of intensive farming call for innovation and investment, not a politics of limits that majorities will reject. On animal suffering itself, this body of work says nothing.

transcript.author: val-plumwood
transcript.about: I endorse it. The honorable harvest asks us to take only what is given, to take with respect, and to give something back. A factory farm takes everything, asks no permission, and returns only waste. That is not a harvest. It treats lives as stock to be stored rather than gifts held in relationship.

transcript.author: val-plumwood
transcript.about: I endorse it, but from entanglement rather than abstract rights. Companion species make each other. Factory farming is a Plantationocene machine: it simplifies animals, workers, and land into units of production and severs every relation of response. Abolition should mean building better ways of living and dying together, not drawing a clean line between humans and animals.

interviews.author: peter-singer
interviews.reaction: Factory farming should be abolished because it inflicts intense suffering on billions of sentient animals for minor human interests such as taste and low prices. Discounting that suffering on the basis of species is speciesism, and land efficiency cannot justify leaving their pain out of the moral sum.

interviews.author: roger-scruton
interviews.reaction: Factory farming should end because it abandons husbandry and cuts the bond of care between farmer, land and animal. The grounds are duties of stewardship and love of home, not animal rights, and the remedy is the good local farm rather than an end to every use of animals.

interviews.author: wendell-berry
interviews.reaction: Factory farming should be abolished because it takes animals off the land, turns manure into pollution and empties the countryside of farmers. The remedy is small mixed farms built on good husbandry, not ending the keeping of animals.

interviews.author: luc-ferry
interviews.reaction: Industrial cruelty toward sentient animals should be curbed and can be banned by democratic law. The grounds are humanist duties toward suffering beings, not rights held by animals or nature, because rights belong only to beings capable of freedom.

interviews.author: ted-nordhaus
interviews.reaction: Abolishing intensive livestock farming would spread animals over far more land and undo decoupling. Its harms call for innovation, such as better intensive systems and meat alternatives, rather than bans that a majority will reject. The work does not address animal suffering.

interviews.author: donna-haraway
interviews.reaction: Factory farming should end because it is a Plantationocene machine. It reduces animals, workers and land to interchangeable units and cuts the ties of mutual response through which species make each other. Abolition means building better ways to live and die together, not drawing a clean line between humans and animals.

interviews.author: val-plumwood
interviews.reaction: Factory farming should be abolished because it is the master's standpoint made industrial. It reduces animals to mindless meat and denies dependence on them. Abolition should not lift humans out of the food chain, since humans are edible too.

interviews.author: baird-callicott
interviews.reaction: Factory farming should end because it degrades the biotic community: it pollutes watersheds, erodes soil and cuts the ties between people, animals and land. The ground is the integrity of the whole, not individual suffering. Mixed farming that fits the land remains defensible.

interviews.author: john-bellamy-foster
interviews.reaction: Factory farming is the metabolic rift at its most extreme. Feed grown on distant land and animals packed into sheds turn soil nutrients into pollution. Abolishing it means bringing animals and land back together and overcoming capitalism's split between town and country.

interviews.author: murray-bookchin
interviews.reaction: Factory farming should be abolished as a social problem before a moral one. Agribusiness turns animals, workers and land into commodities. The remedy is democratic municipalities controlling regional agriculture, not intensification or blaming humanity's consumption habits in general.

interviews.author: jason-hickel
interviews.reaction: Factory farming should be abolished because it is high-throughput production driven by accumulation rather than need. It relies on cheap feed and land from the global South, and intensification cannot decouple it from material and land use fast enough. Rich countries must cut meat production and consumption.

interviews.author: joan-martinez-alier
interviews.reaction: Factory farming should be abolished as an ecological distribution conflict. It pushes manure, polluted water and land seizures for feed crops onto neighbours and Southern communities. Their resistance is an environmentalism of the poor, and intensification only moves the land burden elsewhere.

interviews.author: ramachandra-guha
interviews.reaction: Factory farming should end because it feeds omnivores at the expense of ecosystem people, taking their land, grain and water and leaving them the pollution. Abolition must not become a ban on the herds that pastoralists and peasants depend on for their livelihood.

interviews.author: arne-naess
interviews.reaction: Factory farming should end because every living being has value of its own, apart from its use to humans. Interfering with other life is justified only for vital needs. Affluent overconsumption of meat is not a vital need, while pastoral livelihoods are.

interviews.author: andrew-dobson
interviews.reaction: Factory farming should end because its footprint falls on distant people and lands through imported feed, pollution and emissions. Ecological citizenship makes cutting that footprint a duty of justice, in law and in private conduct. The case for animal citizenship stays open.

interviews.author: timothy-morton
interviews.reaction: Abolition is endorsed, by analogy. No fixed boundary separates species, so turning some beings into stock has no basis. Factory farming also feeds a hyperobject whose emissions and resistant microbes cross every fence, so neither land-sparing nor pastoral nostalgia answers it.

interviews.author: rob-hopkins
interviews.reaction: Factory farming should end because it runs on cheap oil and long supply chains, and energy descent will make it fragile. Communities can start now, without waiting for the state, by rebuilding local, smaller-scale food systems built for resilience.

interviews.author: tom-regan
interviews.reaction: Factory farming must be abolished because animals who are subjects of a life have inherent value and rights that no sum of human benefits can override. Bigger cages and gentler slaughter leave the wrong intact. The same reasoning condemns every use of animals as resources.

interviews.author: carol-j-adams
interviews.reaction: Factory farming should be abolished, but abolition falls short if meat-eating continues. The factory, the small farm and the plate all turn a living animal into an absent referent. Consuming bodies works the same way as the objectification of women.

interviews.author: will-kymlicka
interviews.reaction: Factory farming should be abolished, but that is only the minimum. Domesticated animals are members of a shared society. Justice means turning exploitation into political membership, with their interests represented in law, rather than milder husbandry or cutting all ties with them.

interviews.author: anna-tsing
interviews.reaction: Factory farming is the plantation model applied to animals. It makes bodies, workers and land uniform and interchangeable, and pushes its costs onto distant feed frontiers. It should be abolished, and attention should turn to the entangled ways of living together that can grow in its ruins.

interviews.author: florence-burgat
interviews.reaction: Factory farming should be abolished, but abolition does not go far enough. Eating meat is not a need but a cultural ritual by which humanity defines itself by sacrificing the animal. Kinder husbandry or more efficient production leaves that sacrifice in place.

interviews.author: robin-wall-kimmerer
interviews.reaction: Factory farming should end because it breaks the honorable harvest. It takes everything, asks nothing, gives nothing back, and turns gifts into stock. The wrong is taking without reciprocity, not eating as such, so the remedy is to restore relationship with animals and land.

interviews.author: corine-pelluchon
interviews.reaction: Factory farming should be abolished because the condition of animals is a test of justice. It is a public institution kept alive by law, subsidies and trade rules. Ending it therefore belongs in democratic politics, with phased bans and support for farmers' transition.
